paragraphs: The fairer opponents of the provision on elections in the plan of the Convention will sometimes, when pressed in argument, grant that it is proper. They qualify this, however: it ought to have come with a declaration that all elections must be held in the counties where the electors live. This, they say, was a necessary precaution against abuse of the power. Such a declaration would certainly have done no harm, and to the extent that it quieted apprehensions it might not have been undesirable. But it would in fact have added little or no security against the danger feared. An impartial and judicious examiner will never count its absence as a serious objection to the plan, much less an insuperable one. The views taken of the subject in the two preceding papers must be enough to convince all dispassionate and discerning men of this. If public liberty is ever sacrificed to the ambition of the national rulers, the power under examination, at least, will not be to blame.

Some people are inclined to follow only their jealousy. If they would use it to inspect the individual State constitutions carefully, they would find little less cause for uneasiness and alarm in the latitude most of those constitutions allow on elections than in the latitude proposed for the national government. A review of the State constitutions on this point would go a long way toward removing any ill impressions that remain. But such a review would lead into long and tedious details, so I shall content myself with one example, the State in which I write. The constitution of New York makes no other provision for the LOCALITY of elections than that members of the Assembly shall be elected in the COUNTIES and those of the Senate in the great districts into which the State is or may be divided. There are four such districts at present, each including from two to six counties. It is easy to see that it would be no harder for the legislature of New York to defeat the votes of New York's citizens by confining elections to particular places than for the legislature of the United States to defeat the votes of the citizens of the Union by the same expedient. Suppose, for instance, that the city of Albany were named the sole place of election for the county and district it belongs to. Would not the inhabitants of that city soon become the only electors of the members of both the Senate and the Assembly for that county and district? Can we imagine that electors living in the remote parts of the counties of Albany, Saratoga, Cambridge and so on, or anywhere in the county of Montgomery, would take the trouble to come to Albany to vote for members of the Assembly or Senate sooner than they would go to the city of New York to take part in choosing members of the federal House of Representatives? The alarming indifference we see in the use of so invaluable a privilege under the existing laws, which make every facility available, gives a ready answer. And even apart from any experience, we can have no trouble seeing that when the place of election is at an INCONVENIENT DISTANCE from the elector, the effect on his conduct will be the same whether that distance is twenty miles or twenty thousand miles. Hence it must be clear that objections to the particular form of the federal power to regulate elections apply, in substance, with equal force to the form of the like power in the constitution of this State. For this reason it will be impossible to acquit the one and condemn the other. A similar comparison would lead to the same conclusion about the constitutions of most of the other States.

Someone may say that defects in the State constitutions are no excuse for those in the proposed plan. I answer as follows. No one has ever accused the State constitutions of neglecting the security of liberty. So where the charges thrown at the plan can be shown to apply to them also, the presumption is that those charges are petty quibbles from a predetermined opposition rather than well-founded inferences from a fair search for truth. Some people are willing to treat as innocent omissions in the State constitutions what they regard as unpardonable blemishes in the plan of the Convention. Nothing can be said to them. At most they can be asked to give some substantial reason why the representatives of the people of a single State should be more proof against the lust of power or other sinister motives than the representatives of the people of the United States. If they cannot, they ought at least to prove to us that it is easier to subvert the liberties of three million people, who have local governments to lead their opposition, than those of two hundred thousand people who lack that advantage. And on the point immediately under consideration, they ought to convince us of something else. They must show that it is less probable for a predominant faction in a single State to lean toward a preference for a particular class of electors, in order to maintain its superiority, than for a similar spirit to take hold of the representatives of thirteen States. Those States are spread over a vast region and set apart from each other in several respects by a diversity of local circumstances, prejudices and interests.

So far my observations have aimed only at defending the provision in question on three grounds: theoretical propriety, the danger of placing the power elsewhere, and the safety of placing it as proposed. But I must mention one more thing, a positive advantage that will result from this arrangement and that could not as well have been obtained from any other. I mean the uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives. It is more than possible that experience will prove this uniformity of great importance to the public welfare. It may prove important both as a security against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and as a cure for the diseases of faction. If each State may choose its own time of election, there may be at least as many different times as there are months in the year. The times of election in the individual States, as now fixed for local purposes, range between extremes as far apart as March and November. The result of this diversity would be that the body could never be entirely dissolved or renewed at one time. If an improper spirit of any kind happened to prevail in it, that spirit would tend to pass itself on to the new members as they arrived in succession. The mass would probably stay nearly the same, constantly absorbing its gradual additions into itself. There is a contagion in example that few men have the strength of mind to resist. I am inclined to think that three times the term in office, on condition that the whole body is dissolved at once, might be less dangerous to liberty than one third of that term with gradual and successive changes.
Uniformity in the time of elections seems no less necessary for carrying out the idea of regular rotation in the Senate, and for conveniently assembling the legislature at a fixed time each year.

It may be asked why a time could not have been fixed in the Constitution. The most zealous adversaries of the plan of the Convention in this State are, in general, no less zealous admirers of the State constitution. So the question may be turned back on them: why was no time fixed for the same purpose in the constitution of this State? The best answer is that it was a matter that could safely be left to legislative discretion, and that a time once appointed might, on trial, have proved less convenient than some other. The same answer serves for the question put on the other side. It may be added that the supposed danger of a gradual change is merely speculative. It would hardly have been advisable, on the strength of such speculation, to establish as a fundamental point something that would deprive several States of the convenience of holding the elections for their own governments and for the national government at the same times.
